### Linguistic Metadata

Our genetic data was taken from a range of sources (see Supplementary Table X <!--# This will be a table of where the samples were taken -->). In each case. there was a variant of the question "What is your primary language?". In Y cases, language was inferred based on the village from which the sample was taken. All coding decisions on language names, locations, and the comparability of questions across samples are detailed in the script `processing/format_geneticdata.R`.

```{r echo=FALSE}
if(!file.exists("processed_data/genetic_samples.csv")){
  system("RScript processing/format_geneticdata.R")
}

metadata = read.csv("processed_data/genetic_samples.csv")

## Counts of 
# Gender
g_tble = table(metadata$gender)
names(g_tble)[1] = "Missing"
kable(g_tble, col.names = c("Gender", "Count"))

# Language samples
l_tbl = as.data.frame(table(metadata$interview_language))
colnames(l_tbl) = c("Language", "Samples")
levels(l_tbl$Language)[levels(l_tbl$Language)==""] = "Missing"
l_tbl1 = cbind(l_tbl[1:32,], l_tbl[33:64,])
l_tbl2 = cbind(l_tbl[65:94,], l_tbl[95:124,])
kable(l_tbl1, row.names = NA)
kable(l_tbl2, row.names = NA)

# Language Family samples
lf_tbl = as.data.frame(table(metadata$Branch_Family))
colnames(lf_tbl) = c("Language Family", "Samples")
levels(lf_tbl$`Language Family`)[levels(lf_tbl$`Language Family`)==""] = "Missing"
kable(lf_tbl, row.names = NA)
```

Some decisions of note:

-   Paiwaian is a language which has disputed membership to TNG, and could also be considered as part of the Tereban family [@pawley2017]. We include this language as its own TNG branch, given we have a large sample of speakers (n = 52).

```         
::: {.callout-note}
We could consider Paiwaian as Tereban. SP needs to talk to NE about the strength of evidence for doing this. 
```

-   We have one speaker of Orokolo, an Eleman language that is sometimes categorised as a TNG language. @pawley2017 write there is no evidence for this link. We do not categorise this family as TNG, however, since there is only one individual it is an inconsequential decision for our analysis.

# Building Phylogenies

## Genetic Data

This project uses a set of newly collected genetic samples from Southern New Guinea, collected in 2019 as part of the Papuan Past project, and leverages existing samples drawn from XXX, also collected from the Papuan Past Project.

In total, we analyse a sample of 903 mitogenomes and 72 non-recombinant Y chromosomes (NRY).

## mtDNA

mtDNA samples were sequenced using \[what technology?\] <!--# How was this done? Probably ask Franois-Xavier -->. Sequences are reconstructed tfrom the Revised Cambridge Reference Sequence (rCRS). See script `processing/create_reference_genomes.R` for processing details.

```{r}
if(!file.exists("processed_data/papua_n.fasta") & 
   !file.exists("processed_data/papua_m.fasta")){
  system("RScript processing/create_reference_genomes.R")  
}
```

We have split mtDNA samples into M and N haplotype groups for computational efficiency.

<!--# might exclude the IQTree bit -->

For an initial assessment of appropriate models, we ran IQTree2 [@minh2020]. This command constructs a maximum-likelihood tree for 1000 bootstraps, testing the likelihood of XX models.

```{bash eval = FALSE}
iqtree2 -s ./processed_data/papua_m.fasta -B 1000 -T AUTO
iqtree2 -s ./processed_data/papua_n.fasta -B 1000 -T AUTO
```

These models returned the following results:

We use BEAST v2.7.4 to infer the genealogical relationships between our set of XXX mitogenomes. Here we detail the decisions behind the parameters used for our phylogenetic models, which can also be found in the .xmls file associated with this project.

### Phylogenetic model testing

We test a range of phylogenetic models to understand the phylogenetic structure of the mtDNA in New Guinea.

1.  We use BEAST package bModeltest to assess the most appropriate Substitution model, with Coalescent Bayesian Population model.
2.  We test the following Tree Priors, with a GTR-4 model
    1.  **Coalescent Constant Population - Will be ok with a longer run (mean post = -39250.368)**
    2.  Coalescent Exponental Population - Looks a bit wobbly (mean post = -39219.659)
    3.  Coalescent Bayesian Skyline - Not great
    4.  Coalescent Bayesian Extended Skyline - Not great (post mean = -43148.448)
    5.  Birth-Death - Will be fine with a marignally longer run (mean post = -37512.024)
    6.  Yule Prior - Will be fine with a marignally longer run (mean post = -37508.514)

### Substitution and Site model

We use a General Time Reversible (GTR) model, with a Gamma prior containing four rate categories. A GTR model assumes different rates of change between the all nucleotides, and that those rates are bi-directional (i.e. adenine (A) to guanine (G) occurs at the same rate of G to A). A Gamma prior over the rates allows for rate heterogeneity across sites, with a possibility of four rate categories. The shape parameter is estimated, with a starting value of 1 (default).

Approximately 70% of sites are invariant, so we also implement an invariant sites model, which is estimated from the data. We use empirical base frequencies for each base in this model, and all rates are estimated, except for the CT rate. At least one of the substitutions rates needs to be fixed, because estimating them all leads to model unidentifiability. We fix the transition of CT to 1 in this model, since BEAST scales rates so that the average is 1. Fixing a transition rate is more stable than fixing a transversion rate.

This model can be described as: **GTR+G4+I**

#### Clock model / Mutation Rates

We use a strict clock mutation rate, with a normal prior. Setting a normal prior on the mutation rate means we accommodate uncertainty in the tree-wide rate, but rates do no vary across branches, as is standard with a strict clock.

We determine mtDNA mutations rates from studies calibrating the human mitochondrial clock (@rieux2014, @fu2013). In both studies we consider the whole genome substitution rate. We take the mean mutation rate from both papers to be the mean of the normal prior, and the lowest and highest rates in the range to be the upper and lower values of the distribution.

|             Paper | Estimated Mean Mutation Rate |  Estimated 95% C.I.   |
|------------------:|:----------------------------:|:---------------------:|
|    Fu et al. 2013 |        2.67 x 10^-8^         | 2.16 - 3.16 x 10^-8^  |
| Rieux et al. 2014 |        2.143 x 10^-8^        | 1.58 - 2.706 x 10^-8^ |
|         Used here |       2.4065 x 10^-8^        | 1.58 - 3.16 x 10^-8^  |

To estimate the standard deviation we use the following formula:

$$
SD = \frac{\sqrt{N} * (Upper.CI - Lower.CI)}{t_v(0.05, N) \times 2} 
$$

which gives the result: 1.04 x 10^-8^

### Tree Prior

We use a Coalescent Extended Bayesian Skyline Population history model (EBSP). The EBSP model leverages coalescent theory to account for fluctuating population size in the phylogenetic model, at multiple loci (Heled & Drummond, 2008). The sparsity of historical knowledge in Southern New Guinea means we do not have a good understanding of changes in population size. We opt for using a model that will allow for a fluctuating population, rather than assuming that it did not fluctuate.

### MCMC Settings

We run the tree for 10,000,000 iterations, storing every 10,000 iterations.

# Trait Heritage

To estimate the fidelity of language transmission over time, we calculate the probability of two individuals sharing a language within a genetic clade, across multiple times point in the phylogenetic history. This calculation follow from [@lansing2017].

$$
P(i_l,j_l)|i_{g(t)}, j_{g(t)}) = \frac{P(i_l, j_l \bigcap i_{g(t)}, j_{g(t)})}{P(i_{g(t)}, j_{g(t)}} = \frac{\sum_{g=1}^{c_t}(\sum_{i,j\neq i}1_{cos(l_ig, l_jg) > 0})}{\sum_{g=1}^{c_t}n_g(n_g - 1) / 2}
$$

$c_t$ is the number of genetic clades at any point in history, for t generations. We assume 25 year generation times. $l_{i_g}$ and $l_{j_g}$ are the languages or language families spoken by individuals within genetic clade $g$. $1_{cos(l_{i_g}, l_{i_g}) > 0}$ is 1 if the ith and jth individual share a language, and zero otherwise. $n_g$ is the number of individuals in $g$.

We calculate the trait heritage for a number of different traits.

-   Language of individual

-   Language family of individual

-   Language of individual's father's father

-   Language of individual's mother's mother

-   Language family of individual's father's father

-   Language family of individual's mother's mother

We extend this calculation to calculate the probability of a trait given a further conditions

-   The shared language is a Trans-New Guinea language

-   The shared language is not a Trans-New Guinea language

As with [@lansing2017], we compare the calculated probability with a permuted probability to determine whether languages are more likely to be shared by chance. We calculate XXX permutations per analysis.

We apply the trait heritage function across a posterior of trees. Within each tree we calculate the probability from the data, and the XXX permutations.

The trait heritage functions have been collected into a package that can be found here: <https://github.com/SamPassmore/traitheritage>

## Results

#### Metadata processing

As set out above, we have divided the phylogenetic data into major haplogroups, M & N. For each of these phylogeneies we perform two analyses: the probability of sharing a trait within a genetic clade, and the rate of within and between group variance for all pairs of traits. Traits are analysed at two levels, at the level of the langauge, and at the language clade level. This means for the two analyses, we have four results:

1.  M Haplogroup - Language
2.  M Haplogroup - Language Clade
3.  N Haplogroup - Language
4.  N Haplogroup - Language Clade

```{r}
# Read in the M Haplotype tree
m_tree = read.nexus("NCI/20240528_mtDNA_CCP/CCP-papua_m_noburnin.trees")

# Prune the tree for all individuals for which we have language data for
keep_tips = c(metadata$ID[metadata$haplogroup_MN == "M" & 
                            metadata$ID %in% m_tree[[1]]$tip.label],
              "HGDP00546") # Keep the outgroup label

m_tree = lapply(m_tree, function(t)
  keep.tip(t, keep_tips))

ape::write.nexus(m_tree, file = "NCI/20240528_mtDNA_CCP/CCP-papua_m_noburnin_pruned.trees")

# Save language metadata file
metadata_l = metadata %>% 
  filter(ID %in% keep_tips) %>% 
  select(ID, interview_language)

write.csv(metadata_l, "NCI/R")

# Save language clade metadata file
metadata_lc = metadata %>% 
  filter(ID %in% keep_tips) %>% 
  select(ID, Branch_Family)

```

### Trait heritage

#### mtDNA N Haplotype

```{r echo=FALSE}
mcct_tree_mtdnaN = read.nexus("NCI/mtDNA_N/mtDNA_N-papua_n_daru_pruned.mcct.trees")

language_probability = 
  read.csv("results/Branch_Family_mtDNA_N-papua_n_daru_languagefamily.csv")

permuted_probability = 
  read.csv("results/Branch_Family_mtDNA_N-papua_n_daru_pruned_permuted_languagefamily.csv")

summarizer = function(posterior){
  posterior$generation_time = as.numeric(gsub("g_", replacement = "", posterior$generation))
  posterior %>%
  filter(!is.na(clade_probability)) %>% # remove NA clades. Usually occur because of singleton clades
  group_by(generation_time) %>%
  summarise(mean.prob = mean(clade_probability, na.rm = TRUE),
            ci_hdi = bayestestR::ci(clade_probability), # 95% credible interval
            n_matches = sum(numerator_sum)) %>% 
  tidyr::unpack(ci_hdi)
}

# Summarise the posterior
posterior_summary = summarizer(language_probability)
permuted_summary = summarizer(permuted_probability )

cleaned_tips = gsub("_.*","", mcct_tree_mtdnaN$tip.label)
mcct_tree_mtdnaN$tip.label = cleaned_tips

metadata_ss = metadata[metadata$ID %in% mcct_tree_mtdnaN$tip.label, ]
mcct_tree_mtdnaN = keep.tip(mcct_tree_mtdnaN, metadata_ss$ID[!is.na(metadata_ss$Branch_Family)])

tree_data = full_join(mcct_tree_mtdnaN, metadata_ss, by = c("label" = "ID"))

#### plot 
p_tree = ggtree(tree_data) + 
  geom_tippoint(aes(col = Branch_Family), shape = "\u2588", size = 1.5) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = c(10000, 20000, 30000, 40000),
                     labels = c("10k", "20k", "30k", "40k")) +
  layout_dendrogram() + 
  theme(legend.position = "none", 
        axis.ticks.y = element_line(),
        axis.line.y = element_line(),
        axis.text.y = element_text())

# match scales in each plot
x_range = layer_scales(p_tree)$x$range$range
  
p_prob = ggplot(data = posterior_summary,
                aes(ymin = CI_low, ymax = CI_high, x = generation_time, y = mean.prob)) +
  geom_ribbon(fill = "lightblue", alpha = 0.5) + 
  geom_line(col = "blue") + 
  geom_ribbon(data = permuted_summary, 
              aes(ymin = CI_low, ymax = CI_high, x = generation_time, y = mean.prob),
              fill = "lightgreen", alpha = 0.5) + 
  geom_line(data = permuted_summary, 
              aes(x = generation_time, y = mean.prob),
            col = "forestgreen") + 
  ylim(c(0, 1)) +
  xlim(x_range) + ## max tree height (or max p_tree?)
  coord_flip() +
  xlab("") + 
  ylab("") + 
  # scale_x_continuous(expand = c(0, 0)) + 
  # scale_y_continuous(expand = c(0, 0)) + 
  theme_classic() + 
  theme(panel.grid.major = element_blank(), 
        panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
        panel.background = element_rect(colour = "black", linewidth=0.5))

p_tree + p_prob + 
  plot_layout(widths = c(1, 0.25))

```

These next graphs show the probability of shared language family against geographic proximity. we test geographic proximity at three distances: are two individuals within 50km of each other, 100kms, or 200kms.

```{r}
distance50_probability = read.csv("results/Branch_Family_mtDNA_N-papua_n_daru_distance50.csv")
distance100_probability = read.csv("results/Branch_Family_mtDNA_N-papua_n_daru_distance100.csv")
distance200_probability = read.csv("results/Branch_Family_mtDNA_N-papua_n_daru_distance200.csv")

distance_summary = lapply(list(short = distance50_probability,
                        medium = distance100_probability,
                        long = distance200_probability), 
                        summarizer)

distance_summary = bind_rows(distance_summary, .id = "distance")
distance_summary$distance = factor(distance_summary$distance, 
                                   levels = c("short", "medium", "long"))

facet_names = c(`short` = "w/n 50km",
                `medium` = "w/n 100km",
                `long` = "w/n 200km")

ggplot(data = distance_summary,
       aes(
         ymin = CI_low,
         ymax = CI_high,
         x = generation_time,
         y = mean.prob
       )) +
  geom_ribbon(fill = "lightgreen", alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_line(data = distance_summary,
            aes(x = generation_time, y = mean.prob),
            col = "forestgreen") +
  facet_grid(~ distance, labeller = as_labeller(facet_names)) +
  geom_ribbon(
    data = posterior_summary,
    aes(
      ymin = CI_low,
      ymax = CI_high,
      x = generation_time,
      y = mean.prob
    ),
    fill = "lightblue",
    alpha = 0.5
  ) + geom_line(data = posterior_summary,
                aes(x = generation_time,
                    y = mean.prob),
                col = "blue") +
  scale_x_reverse(breaks = c(0, 10000, 20000, 30000, 40000, 50000),
                  labels = c("0", "10k", "20k", "30k", "40k", "50k")) + 
  xlab("Time (years)") + 
  ylab("Probability") + 
  theme_classic()
  

```

#### mtDNA M: By trait results

```{r}
## Prepare the tree
mcct_tree_mtdnaM = read.nexus("NCI/20240528_mtDNA_CCP/CCP-papua_m_noburnin.mcct.trees")
cleaned_tips = gsub("_.*","", mcct_tree_mtdnaM$tip.label)
mcct_tree_mtdnaM$tip.label = cleaned_tips

metadata_ss = metadata[metadata$ID %in% mcct_tree_mtdnaM$tip.label, ]
mcct_tree_mtdnaM = keep.tip(mcct_tree_mtdnaM, metadata_ss$ID[!is.na(metadata_ss$Branch_Family)])

tree_data = full_join(mcct_tree_mtdnaM, metadata, by = c("label" = "ID"))

## Read in probability data
language_probability = 
  read.csv("results/Branch_Family_CCP-papua_m_noburnin_pruned_languagefamily.csv")

posterior_summary = language_probability %>% 
  mutate(probability = numerator / denominator,
         generation_num = as.numeric(str_remove(generation, "g_"))) %>% 
  group_by(generation_num, posterior) %>% 
  summarise(clade_probability = mean(probability, na.rm = TRUE),
            numerator_sum = sum(numerator)) %>%
  filter(!is.na(clade_probability)) %>% # remove NA clades. Usually occur because of singleton clades
  group_by(generation_num) %>%
  summarise(mean.prob = mean(clade_probability, na.rm = TRUE),
            ci_hdi = bayestestR::ci(clade_probability), # 95% credible interval
            n_matches = sum(numerator_sum)) %>% 
  tidyr::unpack(ci_hdi)

p_tree = ggtree(tree_data) + 
  geom_tippoint(aes(col = Branch_Family), shape = "\u2588", size = 1.5) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = c(10000, 20000, 30000, 40000),
                     labels = c("10k", "20k", "30k", "40k")) +
  layout_dendrogram() + 
  theme(legend.position = "none", 
        axis.ticks.y = element_line(),
        axis.line.y = element_line(),
        axis.text.y = element_text())

# match scales in each plot
x_range = layer_scales(p_tree)$x$range$range
  
p_prob = ggplot(data = posterior_summary,
                aes(ymin = CI_low, ymax = CI_high, x = generation_num, y = mean.prob)) +
  geom_ribbon(fill = "lightblue", alpha = 0.5) + 
  geom_line(col = "blue") + 
  ylim(c(0, 1)) +
  xlim(x_range) + ## max tree height (or max p_tree?)
  coord_flip() +
  xlab("") + 
  ylab("") + 
  # scale_x_continuous(expand = c(0, 0)) + 
  # scale_y_continuous(expand = c(0, 0)) + 
  theme_classic() + 
  theme(panel.grid.major = element_blank(), 
        panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
        panel.background = element_rect(colour = "black", linewidth=0.5))

pp = p_tree + p_prob + 
  plot_layout(widths = c(1, 0.25))

ggsave(plot = pp, filename = "figures/mtDNA_M_CCP_wprob.png", width = 1920, units = "px", height = 1080)
```

## Stable Clades

We further test the correlation between linguistic affiliation and genetic clades by testing trait stability across the posterior sample of trees. To do this, each individual within a phylogeny is assigned a trait. For a particular phylogeny, we identify all genetic clades where the trait is the same between all individuals. We then look across the posterior of phylogeny and identify clades that exist in more than 50% of the posterior (i.e. are stable clades).

#### mtDNA N Haplotypes

```{r}
if(!file.exists("results/mtDNA_N_stableclades.csv")){
  system("RScript analysis/stable_clades.R -t NCI/mtDNA_N/mtDNA_N-papua_n_daru_pruned.trees -v Branch_Family")
}

## Metadata 
metadata = read.csv("processed_data/genetic_samples.csv")

stable_clades_summary = read.csv("results/mtDNA_N_stableclades_summary.csv")

states_df = data.frame(states = metadata$Branch_Family, label = metadata$ID)
states_df = left_join(states_df, metadata[, c("ID", "gender")], by = c("label" = "ID"))

mcct_tree_mtdnaN = read.nexus("NCI/mtDNA_N/mtDNA_N-papua_n_daru_pruned.mcct.trees")

# clean IDs
metadata$ID = gsub("-.*","", metadata$ID)

# subset to taxa in the phylogeny
metadata_ss = metadata[metadata$ID %in% mcct_tree_mtdnaN$tip.label,]

# extract the trait of interest
trait = metadata_ss$Branch_Family
trait[trait == ""] = NA
names(trait) = metadata_ss$ID

# remove missing traits
trait = trait[!is.na(trait)]
trait_df = data.frame(states = factor(trait), label = names(trait))

# match traits and tips
plot_tree = keep.tip(mcct_tree_mtdnaN, names(trait))
plot_tree = ladderize(plot_tree)

nodes = sapply(stable_clades_summary$tips, function(x)
  phytools::findMRCA(plot_tree, tips = unlist(strsplit(x, "; ")))) %>% 
  as.data.frame()
colnames(nodes) = "node"
nodes$tips = rownames(nodes)

# nodes_df = data.frame(nodes = nodes, type = stable_clades_summary$state)
nodes_df = left_join(stable_clades_summary, nodes, by = "tips")

tree_df = tidytree::left_join(plot_tree, trait_df, by = "label") 

## set colours
family_colours = setNames(scales::hue_pal()(17), levels(trait_df$states))

p1 = ggtree(tree_df, layout="roundrect", ladderize = TRUE, mrsd = "2023-01-01") + 
  # geom_tippoint(aes(colour = states), shape = "\u25ac", size = 4.0) +
  geom_tippoint(aes(colour = states), size = 1.0) +
  geom_hilight(data = nodes_df, aes(node = node, fill = state),
               type = "roundrect",
               to.bottom = FALSE) +
  labs(title = "N Haplotypes") + 
  theme_classic(base_size = 20) + 
  scale_color_manual(values = family_colours) + 
  scale_fill_manual(values = family_colours) + 
  guides(color=guide_legend(element_blank()), fill = "none") + 
  theme_tree2() + 
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
p1
ggsave(plot = p1, filename = "figures/stable_clades.pdf")

### Distributions
fit = read.csv("results/mtDNA_N_stableclades_all.csv")
fit = fit %>% 
  dplyr::filter(tips %in% stable_clades_summary$tips)

fit_lines = fit %>%
  group_by(state) %>% 
  summarise(mean_state = mean(Date),
            w_mean = sum(n_tips * Date) / sum(n_tips))

p2 = ggplot(fit, aes(x = Date, y = state, fill = state)) + 
  geom_point(alpha = 0.2) + 
  geom_density_ridges(rel_min_height = 0.01) + 
  scale_fill_manual(values = family_colours) + 
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::comma, breaks = seq(0, 15000, 2500)) + 
  xlab("Years Ago") + 
  ylab(element_blank()) + 
  theme_minimal() + 
  theme(legend.position = "none")
  


p1 + p2 + plot_layout(guides = 'collect', ncol = 2)

```

#### Non-Recombinant Y Chromosomes

### Pairwise Between & Within group variance

We do not only want to understand the probability of particular histories, but also rate at which histories coalesce. To do this, for each pair we calculate the probability of between and within group variance to understand at what point, according to the phylogeny, were two languages groups likely to have been one language group.

This approach extends some assumptions of the phylogenetic model. First, that all partitions are binary.

```{r}
library(data.table)

mcct_tree_mtdnaM = read.nexus("NCI/20240528_mtDNA_CCP/CCP-papua_m_noburnin.mcct.trees")

metadata_ss = metadata[metadata$ID %in% mcct_tree_mtdnaM$tip.label, ]
trait = metadata_ss$Branch_Family
names(trait) = metadata_ss$ID

w_b = traitheritage::within_between(tree = mcct_tree_mtdnaM, generation_time = 25, trait = trait)

saveRDS(w_b, "results/Branch_Family_mtDNAM_CCP_withinbetween.RDS")
w_b = readRDS("results/Branch_Family_mtDNAM_CCP_withinbetween.RDS")

v_within = w_b$v_within
v_within[,  generation_num := as.numeric(str_remove(generation, "g_")),]
setkey(v_within, trait)

kainantu_chumbu_w = v_within[J(c("Chimbu-Wahgi", "Kainantu-Goroka"))]

v_between = w_b$v_between
v_between[,  generation_num := as.numeric(str_remove(generation, "g_")),]
setkey(v_between, trait_pairs)

kainantu_chumbu_b = v_between[J(c("Chimbu-WahgiKainantu-Goroka"))]


ggplot() + 
  geom_line(data = kainantu_chumbu_w, 
            aes(x = generation_num, y = v_within, col = trait)) + 
  geom_line(data = kainantu_chumbu_b,
            aes(x = generation_num, y = v_between)) + 
  ylab("Probability") + 
  xlab("Time") + 
  theme_classic()


ggplot(data = v_within, aes(x = generation_num, y = v_within, col = trait)) + 
  geom_line() + 
  facet_wrap(~trait) + 
  theme(legend.position = "none")
  
branch = "Chimbu-Wahgi"

v_between_particular = v_between[,.SD[stringr::str_detect(trait_pairs, branch)],]

ggplot(data = v_between_particular, 
       aes(x = generation_num, y = v_between, col = trait_pairs)) + 
  geom_line() + 
  facet_wrap(~trait_pairs) + 
  geom_line(data = v_within[J(branch)], 
             aes(x = generation_num, y = v_within, col = trait),
            col = "grey40", lwd = 0.5) + 
  theme_light() +
  theme(legend.position = "none") 


```
